body:
Nandalal Bose and the development of Indian art education

Nandalal Bose (1882–1966) was an important student of Abanindranath Tagore. He carried forward the effort to develop modern Indian art through close engagement with Indian artistic traditions.

He was invited by Rabindranath Tagore to lead art education at Kala Bhavana, Santiniketan, which became associated with Visva-Bharati. Santiniketan provided an important setting in which artists explored Indian art, nature, village life and the relationship between artistic expression and society.

It is necessary to distinguish the 2 members of the Tagore family. Abanindranath Tagore was the leading founder of the Bengal School. Rabindranath Tagore established the wider Santiniketan educational environment with which Kala Bhavana became associated.

The Haripura Posters and their Gujarat connection

One of Nandalal Bose's best-known contributions was the series called the Haripura Posters. These works were prepared for the 1938 Indian National Congress session at Haripura in Gujarat, following an invitation from Mahatma Gandhi.

The paintings presented ordinary people engaged in familiar activities. Subjects included farmers, drummers, craftspeople and women performing everyday tasks. They used simplified forms, lively lines and colours inspired by Indian folk-art traditions.

The Haripura Posters are important because they expressed the dignity of ordinary labour and village life. Their subjects differed from the royal portraits and epic scenes associated with Raja Ravi Varma.

Haripura is in Gujarat. The Haripura Posters connect Nandalal Bose, Mahatma Gandhi and the 1938 Congress session with a significant episode in modern Indian painting.

Why the posters were modern paintings

The posters were inspired by folk-art forms, but they were modern artworks created for a specific public occasion. Their purpose was to communicate familiar aspects of Indian life to a broad audience. They demonstrate how a modern painter could learn from traditional art without merely copying an older painting.

Other painters and their works

Kshitindranath Majumdar

Kshitindranath Majumdar was associated with the artistic direction established by Abanindranath Tagore. His painting Rasa-Lila is an example of a work that connects Indian cultural subject matter with the artistic interests of the Bengal School.

M. R. Chughtai

M. R. Chughtai was another painter influenced by the artistic developments associated with the Bengal School. His painting Radhika is among the works identified with this period.

Jamini Roy

Jamini Roy (1887–1972) developed a distinctive modern painting style inspired by the folk painting traditions of Bengal. Although he received academic training, he moved away from European academic realism and adopted simplified figures, strong outlines and flat areas of colour.

His subjects included village life, women and children. His approach made paintings appear direct and visually accessible.

Jamini Roy belongs to the wider history of modern painting in Bengal, but his mature folk-inspired style should not be confused with the wash-based approach commonly associated with Abanindranath Tagore.

Distinguishing the principal contributions

ArtistPrincipal associationRecognisable example
Abanindranath TagoreLeading founder of Bengal SchoolBharat Mata; Journey's End
Nandalal BoseKala Bhavana, SantiniketanHaripura Posters
Kshitindranath MajumdarBengal School artistic traditionRasa-Lila
M. R. ChughtaiBengal School influenceRadhika
Jamini RoyModern folk-inspired paintingPaintings of village life, women and children

Prelims focus

  • Nandalal Bose studied under Abanindranath Tagore.
  • Nandalal Bose was associated with Kala Bhavana at Santiniketan.
  • The Haripura Posters were prepared for the 1938 Congress session in Gujarat.
  • Mahatma Gandhi invited Nandalal Bose to produce the Haripura works.
  • Kshitindranath Majumdar is associated with Rasa-Lila; M. R. Chughtai with Radhika.
  • Trap: Jamini Roy's mature folk-inspired style should not be treated as identical to Abanindranath Tagore's wash-based painting.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12, An Introduction to Indian Art—Part II, Chapter 6, pp. 87–90 and 91–97, reprint 2025–26; National Gallery of Modern Art, Rediscovering Haripura Panels: Nandalal Bose, and collection records for Haripura paintings, accessed 23 November 2026; National Portal and Digital Repository for Museums of India, Nandalal Bose collection descriptions, accessed 23 November 2026.]

title: Nandalal Bose, Santiniketan and Other Important Painters of the Bengal School Period

body:
The development of modern painting in Gujarat

Modern painting in Gujarat developed through the work of individual artists, art teachers, cultural publications and educational institutions. Artists from Gujarat studied both Indian and European-influenced artistic methods. They also helped establish organisations through which painting could reach students and the wider public.

Among the important names associated with this development are Ravishankar Raval, Rasiklal Parikh and Rameshbhai Pandya.

Ravishankar Raval: Kalaguru of Gujarat

Ravishankar Raval (1892–1977), also written as Ravishankar Rawal, was a major figure in the development of modern painting and art education in Gujarat. He is popularly known as Kalaguru, meaning a respected teacher or master of art.

Raval studied at the Sir J. J. School of Art in Bombay, now Mumbai. He subsequently made Ahmedabad the principal centre of his artistic activities.

Bilvamangala and the Bombay Art Society

One of his notable paintings was Bilvamangala. It received a gold medal at the Bombay Art Society's annual exhibition.

The work is associated with Rajput-inspired painting, particularly in its use of relatively flat areas of colour. This illustrates an important point: a modern Gujarati painter could draw upon an older Indian artistic tradition while creating work in the modern period.

The Kumar magazine

Raval started the Gujarati monthly magazine Kumar in 1924. The publication became an important means of encouraging interest in art and literature, introducing readers to artistic work and helping develop a wider cultural audience.

He also established Gujarat Kala Sangh in Ahmedabad, contributing to the teaching and promotion of art. His importance therefore extends beyond the paintings he produced personally.

Ravishankar Raval: Kalaguru; Bilvamangala; Bombay Art Society gold medal; Kumar monthly, 1924; Gujarat Kala Sangh, Ahmedabad.

Rasiklal Parikh: Painting and art education

Rasiklal Parikh (1910–1982) was another important Gujarati painter. He was associated with Rajpipla in present-day Narmada district.

Parikh initially studied drawing under Ravishankar Raval. He later pursued further artistic training in Madras, Bombay and Santiniketan. His education reflects the connections between Gujarat and other important centres of Indian art.

He became known particularly for paintings using the wash technique. His subjects included women and children, whose expressions and everyday qualities he represented with sensitivity. He also worked in other artistic media, including watercolour and printmaking.

Parikh contributed to art education in Ahmedabad. He became associated with the art-teacher training institution known as Kalashala at Sheth C. N. Vidyalaya, established in 1951, and served as its first principal.

Rasiklal Parikh's career illustrates how one artist could connect several forms of contribution: learning from a Gujarati teacher, studying at major Indian art centres, producing paintings and training future art teachers.

Rameshbhai Pandya

Rameshbhai Pandya is also identified among the notable painters of Gujarat in state-board cultural-history coverage. At the prelims level, his name should be recognised as part of Gujarat's modern painting tradition, alongside Ravishankar Raval and Rasiklal Parikh.

The principal factual associations to remember are strongest for Raval and Parikh: Raval's Bilvamangala, Kumar and Gujarat Kala Sangh; and Parikh's connection with Rajpipla, Raval, the wash technique and art education.

Distinguishing Gujarat's modern painting from folk painting

Pithora painting belongs to the study of Gujarat's folk and tribal artistic traditions. It should be classified under folk art, rather than treated as a modern painting school founded by Raval, Parikh or another academic painter.

Connections across the subtopic

The development of modern Indian painting can be understood through 3 connected but distinct histories. Raja Ravi Varma joined Indian subject matter with European-influenced realism and received Gaekwad patronage in Baroda. The Bengal School, led by Abanindranath Tagore, sought an Indian artistic identity through the study of Indian painting traditions. Gujarati painters, including Ravishankar Raval and Rasiklal Parikh, developed artistic work and art education in Gujarat.

There was also a direct connection between the Bengal School period and Gujarat through Nandalal Bose's Haripura Posters, created for the 1938 Congress session in Gujarat. These connections show why the location of an artist's birth, the place where an artwork was commissioned and the region associated with a painting movement should be considered separately.

Prelims focus

  • Ravishankar Raval is popularly known as Kalaguru.
  • His painting Bilvamangala received a gold medal at the Bombay Art Society's annual exhibition.
  • Raval began the Gujarati monthly Kumar in 1924.
  • Rasiklal Parikh was associated with Rajpipla and studied under Raval.
  • Parikh is especially associated with the wash technique and art education.
  • Trap: Pithora is a folk-art tradition, not an academic school of modern Indian painting.

[Sources: GSEB Solutions, Class 8 Social Science, Chapter 7, Art in Modern India, questions on Gujarat painters, Ravishankar Raval, Bilvamangala, Kumar and Gujarat Kala Sangh, accessed 23 November 2026; Census of India 2011, District Census Handbook: Narmada, Part XII-A, Analytical Note, p. 101, Rasiklal Parikh; Aakriti Art Gallery, The Forgotten Pioneer: Rasiklal Parikh, 2011, accessed 23 November 2026; The Times of India, Raval, an Artist Par Excellence, 18 August 2010; National Gallery of Modern Art, Rediscovering Haripura Panels: Nandalal Bose, accessed 23 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Three branches connect modern Indian painters with their art and Gujarat links, while Pithora is shown separately as folk art.
pictures.caption: Modern Indian painting connected artists, patrons, institutions and regions in different ways.

title: Modern Painters of Gujarat: Ravishankar Raval, Rasiklal Parikh and Their Legacy
